title: Mastery Challenge: How Government Works
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of How Government Works Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from why governments exist to your own part in one: authority, taxes, the social contract, citizenship, duties, local councils, news and the civil service. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The How Government Works Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions, from why governments exist to your own part in one. Level 1 began with a sailor's word for steering a ship; now you're the one at the helm. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: How Government Works: mastered
learned: Why governments exist and how they're paid for
Authority, law and the social contract
Taking part: councils, representatives and the news

questions.prompt: Mastery: the word "government" goes back to a Greek verb for which everyday job?

options.label: Counting a harvest
options.rationale: The root is nautical, not agricultural.

options.label: Guarding a gate
options.rationale: Not the root: it's steering.

options.label: Writing a law
options.rationale: Laws came later; the word means steering.

questions.explanation: Through Latin gubernare, "govern" comes from the Greek kybernan: to steer or pilot a ship.

questions.prompt: A robber and a traffic officer can both make you stop. What does only the officer have, in Weber's terms?

options.label: More physical strength
options.rationale: Strength is power, not authority.

options.label: Authority: power people accept as legitimate
Charisma that people admire
options.rationale: Charisma is one source of authority, but acceptance is the key.

options.label: A weapon
options.rationale: The robber may have one too. That's power.

questions.explanation: Authority is accepted power: people follow it because they see it as legitimate.

questions.prompt: Level 5's free riders and Level 94's volunteers are near opposites. Why?

options.label: Both are paid by government
options.rationale: Neither is: free riders pay nothing, volunteers give for free.

options.label: Free riders give time; volunteers give money
options.rationale: It's the other way round, roughly.

options.label: Free riders take without paying; volunteers give without being required
Both are required by law
options.rationale: Volunteer work is non-compulsory by definition.

questions.explanation: Free riders enjoy a public good without paying; volunteers give unpaid time that no one can make them give.

questions.prompt: You pay a bus fare and a tax. By the OECD's definition, what makes the tax different?

options.label: It is optional, like a tip
options.rationale: Taxes are compulsory.

options.label: It buys you one specific service
options.rationale: That's the fare. Taxes are unrequited.

options.label: It is always a fixed amount
options.rationale: Taxes vary with what they fall on.

options.label: It is compulsory and buys nothing in particular

questions.explanation: Taxes are compulsory and unrequited: what you get back isn't in proportion to what you paid, unlike a fare.

questions.prompt: Canada's citizenship guide says rights come with responsibilities. Which Level 7 idea says much the same?

options.label: The social contract, setting out rights and duties of each side
Weber's charismatic authority
options.rationale: That's about a leader's personal qualities.

options.label: The free rider problem
options.rationale: That's about public goods, not duties.

options.label: Hammurabi's eye for an eye
options.rationale: That's a penalty, not a rights-and-duties bargain.

questions.explanation: A social contract sets out the rights and duties of ruled and rulers: rights with responsibilities attached.

questions.prompt: A baby born abroad to a Japanese mother is a Japanese citizen. Which rule is that?

options.label: Jus soli, the right of the soil
options.rationale: The baby was born abroad, so birthplace isn't the reason.

options.label: Jus sanguinis, the right of blood
Naturalization
options.rationale: Naturalization is for people who apply later.

options.label: The general will
options.rationale: That's Rousseau, not a citizenship rule.

questions.explanation: Japan uses descent: a child is Japanese if the father or mother is a Japanese national at birth.

questions.prompt: A council meeting in Canada is debating water supply and public transit. Which level of government is it?

options.label: Federal
options.rationale: The federal level handles things like defence and currency.

options.label: Provincial or territorial
options.rationale: Provinces run schools and hospitals.

options.label: International
options.rationale: These are local services.

questions.explanation: Canada's municipal governments handle local services like water supply, transit, parks, waste and local roads.

questions.prompt: Which country made voting at federal elections a legal duty in 1924?

options.label: Canada
options.rationale: Canada's guide lists voting as a responsibility; the 1924 law was Australia's.

options.label: Japan
options.rationale: Japan appeared in Level 91 for citizenship, not voting.

options.label: The United Kingdom
options.rationale: Not the example: it was Australia.

questions.explanation: Australia made voting at federal elections compulsory in 1924.

questions.prompt: A newspaper piece is clearly labeled "Comment". By the journalism codes in Level 95, what is it?

options.label: A correction of an earlier error
options.rationale: Corrections fix mistakes; this is opinion.

options.label: Opinion, kept distinct from factual reporting
A breach of the code
options.rationale: Labeled comment is exactly what the codes ask for.

options.label: An advertisement
options.rationale: Ads are a different category.

questions.explanation: Both codes ask outlets to label commentary and distinguish comment from fact. The label tells you it's opinion.

questions.prompt: UK civil servants serve any elected government equally well. Which of Weber's kinds of authority does that reflect?

options.label: Traditional
options.rationale: Traditional authority rests on custom, like inherited thrones.

options.label: Charismatic
options.rationale: Charisma belongs to a person, not an office.

options.label: None: civil servants hold only power
options.rationale: They work within legal-rational authority.

questions.explanation: Legal-rational authority belongs to the office, not the person, so civil servants serve whoever holds office.
